stories.title: Provident Lands Financing for 1.3M-SF Baytown Venture
stories.excerpt: Provident Realty Advisors has obtained financing for the construction of Phase II of Port 99, a 1.3 million square foot, three-building industrial venture in Baytown, near the Port of Houston. PGIM’s Real Estate Investment Group provided a $30.4 million mezzanine construction loan. The mezzanine loan was provided alongside senior financing from Bank OZK, with Northmarq arranging the debt financing and joint-venture equity provided by Junction Commercial Real Estate. The project’s costs are estimated at $124 million. The project expands Provident Realty Advisors’ Port 99 development following the successful lease-up of Phase I and is designed to serve continued demand from port-dependent logistics, distribution, and manufacturing users. PGIM’s Daniel Kattan added, “Houston remains one of the country’s most attractive industrial markets, supported by its strategic location, world-class logistics infrastructure, and long-term economic growth.” The post Provident Lands Financing for 1.3M-SF Baytown Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Provident Realty Advisors secures $30.4M mezzanine loan from PGIM for Port 99 Phase II in Baytown, Texas.
1.3M-SF industrial project with $124M total cost expanding after successful Phase I lease-up.
Port of Houston logistics demand driving continued industrial development in strategic gateway market.
stories.summary: Provident Realty Advisors has closed $30.4 million in mezzanine financing from PGIM's Real Estate Investment Group for Phase II of Port 99, a 1.3 million square foot, three-building industrial venture in Baytown near the Port of Houston. The project carries a total development cost of $124 million and builds on the successful lease-up of Phase I. The expansion reflects sustained demand from port-dependent logistics, distribution, and manufacturing tenants seeking Houston's superior gateway infrastructure.
stories.impact: This signals robust industrial demand in the Houston logistics corridor remains resilient and capital is available for high-quality port-proximate projects. However, industrial supply growth is accelerating (see article 2); multifamily developers should monitor whether logistics employment growth in Baytown/Houston sublets translate to residential demand or if industrial saturation erodes rents in adjacent submarkets.

stories.title: INDUS Acquires 757K-SF Houston Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Equus Capital Partners sold Park 845 Crossing, a 757,325-square-foot Class A multi-tenant industrial portfolio located at 11710 North Freeway in Houston. INDUS Realty Trust acquired the asset. Constructed between 2008 and 2014, Park 845 Crossing comprises five concrete tilt-wall buildings situated on 38.9 acres at the interchange of Interstate 45 and Beltway 8. The portfolio offers a mix of rear-load and cross-dock configurations, with individual buildings ranging from approximately 54,000 to 245,000 square feet and clear heights from 18 to 30 feet. At the time of sale, the property was 99% leased to 11 tenants across a range of industrial categories — including foodservice distribution, tire manufacturing and distribution, HVAC wholesale, third-party logistics and airfreight services. The JLL Capital Markets team representing Equus was led by Trent Agnew and Charlie Strauss, along with Lance Young, Brooke Petzold and Max Myers. The post INDUS Acquires 757K-SF Houston Industrial Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: INDUS Realty Trust acquires Park 845 Crossing, 757K-SF Class A industrial portfolio at I-45/Beltway 8 in Houston.
Five-building property 99% leased to 11 tenants; constructed 2008–2014 with clear heights 18–30 feet.
Equus Capital Partners exit signals institutional appetite for stabilized, fully-leased gateway logistics assets.
stories.summary: INDUS Realty Trust has acquired Park 845 Crossing, a 757,325 square foot Class A multi-tenant industrial portfolio located at the I-45/Beltway 8 interchange in Houston, from Equus Capital Partners. The five-building property comprises concrete tilt-wall structures on 38.9 acres, delivered between 2008 and 2014, with rear-load and cross-dock configurations. At closing, the portfolio was 99% leased to 11 tenants across foodservice distribution, tire manufacturing, HVAC wholesale, and logistics.
stories.impact: The sale of a fully-leased, stabilized industrial asset at a prime logistics node to an institutional buyer indicates capital-flow strength but also market maturity in Houston industrial. Combined with Provident's new Phase II start (article 1), Houston's industrial supply pipeline is thickening; multifamily developers should watch for wage pressure and cost inflation as construction activity concentrates and labor competes across sectors.

stories.title: PGIM Loans $83M to Refi 325-Unit New Jersey Apartment Complex
stories.excerpt: The final piece to a 1,300-unit apartment portfolio refinancing has been sealed. Commercial Observer can first report that Capodagli Property Company has secured $82.6 million to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10, a 325-unit Class A multifamily complex in Roselle, N.J. PGIM provided the debt, structured as a bridge loan, while Greystone Capital Advisors’ Drew Fletcher, Bryan Grover, Miryam Reinitz-Kops and Jesse Kopecky arranged the transaction. The deal follows $287 million in cross-collateralized bridge financing PGIM had provided for four other Class A, multifamily assets in New Jersey throughout 2025. In total, PGIM provided $369.5 million in debt for a 1,340-unit multifamily portfolio comprised of Meridia Village Commons at 209 Valley Street in South Orange, N.J.; Meridia Pompton Lakes at 61 Wanaque Avenue in Pompton Lakes, N.J.; Meridia Linden 1001 at 1001 West Elizabeth Avenue in Linden, N.J.; and Meridia Little Ferry at 110 Bergen Turnpike in Little Ferry, N.J. Meridia Roselle Park 10 is at 10 West Westfield Avenue in Roselle Park, N.J., a suburb not far from Newark Liberty International Airport and 25 miles southwest of Times Square in Manhattan. Greystone’s Fletcher said in a statement that by breaking the cross-collateralized structure into separate deals, Capodagli Property Company was able to refinance each asset “on consistent terms as each came online,” giving each deal flexibility to seek out permanent financing at its own rate. “Completing this facility reflects the strength of our long-term relationship with Capodagli and PGIM’s continued conviction in their platform,” said Fletcher. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobsever.com.
bullets: PGIM closes $82.6M bridge loan to Capodagli for 325-unit Meridia Roselle Park 10 in Roselle Park, New Jersey.
Part of $369.5M cross-collateralized financing for 1,340-unit New Jersey multifamily portfolio across five Class A assets.
Bridge structure and portfolio refinancing signal potential valuation or rate-environment stress in Northeast multifamily.
stories.summary: Capodagli Property Company has secured $82.6 million in bridge financing from PGIM to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10, a 325-unit Class A apartment complex in Roselle Park, New Jersey. This closing completes a $369.5 million cross-collateralized bridge financing package PGIM provided in early 2025 for five Meridia-branded Class A multifamily assets across New Jersey totaling 1,340 units in South Orange, Pompton Lakes, Linden, Little Ferry, and Roselle Park.
stories.impact: Bridge financing on this scale for stabilized New Jersey multifamily suggests either refinancing pressure tied to maturity walls or active cap-rate compression play by Capodagli. The concentration of one lender across a five-asset portfolio in a constrained market (limited acquisition inventory, high construction costs) may signal capital scarcity or lender appetite for control; multifamily developers eyeing Northern New Jersey should track refinancing velocity and exit timing for signal on market timing and rate expectations.

stories.title: Mamdani Wants to Add 18K New Homes on Staten Island
stories.excerpt: There’s a joke about how Staten Island got its name. Dutch settlers sailing into New York Harbor saw the 14-mile land mass and exclaimed “Is zat an island?” (You have to read it with the accent.) Is it the reality of how one of New York City boroughs got its name? No, but as the saying goes, “When the legend becomes fact, print the legend.” Fast forward to 2026, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has some big plans for the little island across the harbor from Manhattan. He is hoping to see a 9.5 percent growth in new homes on Staten Island over the next five years, or about 17,675 new homes across the borough, according to a growth plan from the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) released Wednesday. “As the city commits to ambitious housing action through the Block by Block plan, the draft Fair Housing Growth Strategy provides a framework for measuring need and understanding where we should grow, with fair housing at its center,” Sideya Sherman, director of the Department of City Planning, said in a statement. Staten Island is broken up in three segments: North Shore, Mid-Island and South Shore. The South Shore and Mid-Island are the island’s least dense areas. However, residents and elected officials on the South Shore have historically pushed back on more residential development in their neighborhoods, so the mayor could be facing an uphill battle. “Staten Island is probably the most perfect place in the world because you’re 20 or 40 minutes away from the largest city in the country, but at the same time it’s like being in New England,” Stuart Saft, a real estate lawyer with Holland & Knight, previously told Commercial Observer. “I’ve been to Staten Island, and it’s a magnificent place to be.” The mayor isn’t just targeting housing growth on Staten Island over the next five years, mind you. bullets: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani targets 17,675 new homes on Staten Island over five years (9.5% growth).
Citywide 'Block by Block' plan and Fair Housing Growth Strategy framework directing housing production targets.
Policy shift signals regulatory green light and city resources behind least-developed NYC borough.
stories.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released a Fair Housing Growth Strategy through the Department of Housing Preservation and Development targeting 17,675 new homes across Staten Island over the next five years, representing 9.5% growth. The plan is part of the broader citywide 'Block by Block' housing action and aims to address housing need with fair housing at its center, providing a framework for measuring demand and directing growth.
stories.impact: This is a major signal that City Hall is actively de-risking Staten Island as a development destination through policy legitimation and may include land contributions, tax abatements, or expedited review. For multifamily developers, this is a window to acquire sites and begin pre-development before land prices spike and competition intensifies. However, execution risk is high; monitor HPD funding levels, CEQR timelines, and community opposition, as political commitments often exceed delivery.

stories.title: Mooresville Industrial Park Trades for $135M
stories.excerpt: A Blackstone affiliate sold the North Charlotte Commerce Center in Mooresville to CBRE Investment Management for $135 million. The Charlotte Business Journal reports the deal was part of a 2.3-million-square-foot portfolio sale that also included industrial parks in two other states. CBRE IM is an independently operated affiliate of CBRE Group. The North Charlotte Commerce Center is a three-building industrial park at 134 Serviceberry Way, 142 Serviceberry Way and 156 Exmore Road. It spans over 900,000 square feet. Strategic Real Estate Partners developed it on behalf of Blackstone’s Link Logistics. The building at 142 Serviceberry Way is the newest — and the largest — of the three, at 723,533 square feet. It was delivered in May 2024. The other buildings are 113,000 square feet and 90,000 square feet, and were delivered in 2022 and 2023 respectively. The post Mooresville Industrial Park Trades for $135M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Blackstone affiliate (Link Logistics) sells North Charlotte Commerce Center in Mooresville to CBRE Investment Management for $135M.
900K-SF three-building industrial park; newest building (723K SF) delivered May 2024; 99%+ occupancy.
Blackstone industrial exit via secondary market sale signals opportune exit window and valuation clarity post-delivery.
stories.summary: A Blackstone affiliate sold the North Charlotte Commerce Center in Mooresville, North Carolina to CBRE Investment Management for $135 million as part of a 2.3 million square foot multi-state industrial portfolio sale. The property comprises three concrete tilt-wall buildings totaling over 900,000 square feet on 38.9 acres at a strategic I-85 node. The newest and largest building (723,533 SF) was delivered in May 2024, with the other two buildings delivered in 2022 and 2023.
stories.impact: Blackstone's sale of recently stabilized industrial (post-May 2024 delivery) to CBRE IM signals capitulation on industrial hold/value-add thesis or rebalancing of portfolio risk. This suggests cap rates are rationalizing post-delivery and newer industrial is less attractive at current pricing. Multifamily developers in Charlotte/Piedmont region should monitor industrial cap-rate compression; if it persists, it signals labor availability and wage growth in logistics, which may support apartment demand but raise construction costs.

stories.title: Sandy Springs Okays Incentives for Mall Redevelopment
stories.excerpt: The City of Sandy Springs approved an incentive package to support Woodfield Development’s transformation of North River Shopping Center. The approval advances Woodfield’s planned redevelopment of the aging commercial center into a new mixed-use neighborhood featuring 336 multifamily residences, 85 for-sale townhomes, retail, restaurants and a new public park. Woodfield Development has approximately eight acres of the 13-acre North River Shopping Center site at 8830 Roswell Road under contract and will spearhead the redevelopment. To help advance the project and its community benefits, City Council approved targeted incentives.    The incentives include waiving the City’s recreation impact and permit fees, as well as a recommendation for the Sandy Springs Development Authority to authorize a 10-year property tax abatement. Together, the incentives are valued at just over $4.3 million and are contingent upon demolition of the existing shopping center and construction of the approved redevelopment and City park by Woodfield Development. Construction is expected to begin later this year. The post Sandy Springs Okays Incentives for Mall Redevelopment appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Sandy Springs, Georgia approves $4.3M incentive package for Woodfield Development's North River Shopping Center redevelopment.
336-unit multifamily, 85 townhomes, retail, and new public park on 13-acre site; 10-year property tax abatement.
City waives impact and permit fees; incentives contingent on demolition and delivery of approved plan.
stories.summary: The City of Sandy Springs approved a targeted incentive package valued at just over $4.3 million to support Woodfield Development's redevelopment of North River Shopping Center at 8830 Roswell Road. The mixed-use project includes 336 multifamily units, 85 for-sale townhomes, retail, restaurants, and a new public park on approximately eight acres of the 13-acre site. Incentives include waived recreation impact and permit fees and a recommendation for a 10-year property tax abatement.
stories.impact: This is a clear municipal signal that infill mixed-use redevelopment of aging retail corridors is a priority in Sandy Springs' submarket. The 10-year tax abatement and fee waivers substantially reduce basis and improve underwriting, making the deal feasible. Multifamily developers should identify similar aging retail/shopping-center sites in Sandy Springs and nearby North Atlanta markets and approach municipalities about pre-approved incentive frameworks; tax abatements at this scale can shift returns by 100–150 bps.

stories.title: Finmarc Acquires 460K-SF North Virginia Office Portfolio for $77M
stories.excerpt: Finmarc Management, Inc. has completed the $77.5 million acquisition of Highline at Greensboro, a two-building portfolio composed of approximately 460,000 square feet of commercial office space. The property consists of 8401 and 8405 Greensboro Drive, twin, 10-story office towers located in the Tysons Corner submarket of Northern Virginia, and were 70 percent leased and occupied at the time of the sales transaction. Cushman & Wakefield’s Paul Collins and Kevin Sidney represented the seller, CIM Group. Aaron Rosenfeld of Kelley Drye & Warren LLP provided legal services to Finmarc and Cliff Mendelson of Metropolis Capital Advisors assisted in the debt placement.The ten-story buildings totaling 460,000 square feet are comprised of 8401 Greensboro and 8405 Greensboro. The property is served by The Boro, a walkable amenity anchored by Whole Foods Market which includes 250,000 square feet of retail space featuring a diverse range of sit-down and fast-casual restaurants. The post Finmarc Acquires 460K-SF North Virginia Office Portfolio for $77M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Finmarc Management acquires Highline at Greensboro, 460K-SF twin office towers in Tysons Corner submarket for $77.5M.
Two 10-story buildings (8401 and 8405 Greensboro Drive) were 70% leased at time of sale.
CIM Group off-load at $77.5M signals office cap-rate softness; Tysons office market challenged post-pandemic.
stories.summary: Finmarc Management has completed the $77.5 million acquisition of Highline at Greensboro, a two-building office portfolio totaling approximately 460,000 square feet in the Tysons Corner submarket of Northern Virginia. The twin 10-story office towers at 8401 and 8405 Greensboro Drive were 70% leased and occupied at the time of sale. CIM Group was the seller.
stories.impact: This low 70% occupancy rate at sale and Finmarc's entry (typically a value-add/stabilization player) signal continued office weakness in Northern Virginia despite Tysons' reputation as a premier corporate submarket. Limited multifamily relevance here, but office distress near major employment nodes can displace workers, suppress residential demand in nearby apartments, and reduce rents—particularly in Tysons-proximate submarkets.

stories.title: Planet Fitness Takes 15K SF at Coney Island Residential Development
stories.excerpt: Wake up, it’s time for a workout. Planet Fitness has inked a 14,500-square-foot retail lease at the base of a new residential tower in Coney Island, Brooklyn, with Cammeby’s International Group and Rybak Development. Planet Fitness will move into the space at 532 Neptune Avenue next year on a 10-year lease with an asking rent of $65 per square foot, according to the New York Business Journal, which first reported the deal. Planet Fitness was represented by CBRE, while ownership was represented by Commercial Acquisitions. The names of the brokers on both sides of the deal were not immediately available. The brokerages did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. Planet Fitness has nearly 50 gyms in New York City across all five boroughs. The company did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. Cammeby’s and Rybak completed the three-tower, 499-unit residential complex at 532 Neptune late last year, featuring studio to three-bedroom homes. Some 30 percent of those units are designated as affordable housing. The development has 758,600 square feet of residential space, 40,368 square feet of ground-floor commercial space and 20,722 square feet of community facilities. The two developers aren’t stopping their work in Coney Island anytime soon, either, as Cammeby’s and Rybak submitted a rezoning application in March to build two 22-story residential buildings with a total of 703 units at 3030 Ocean Parkway and 400 Neptune Avenue. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Planet Fitness signs 14,500-SF lease at 532 Neptune Avenue, Coney Island, Brooklyn base retail; $65/SF asking rent.
10-year lease term at three-tower, 499-unit residential complex delivered late 2024 by Cammeby's and Rybak.
Anchor tenant activation validates ground-floor retail in new residential; 30% affordability suggests mixed-income demand signal.
stories.summary: Planet Fitness has leased 14,500 square feet of retail space at the base of a new residential tower at 532 Neptune Avenue in Coney Island, Brooklyn, on a 10-year lease at $65 per square foot asking rent. The space is part of a completed three-tower, 499-unit residential complex delivered late 2024 by Cammeby's International Group and Rybak Development. The property features studio to three-bedroom units with approximately 30% affordability.
stories.impact: Planet Fitness's commitment validates retail-anchored residential development in Coney Island and de-risks the ground-floor economics for future similar projects in outer boroughs. The 30% affordability means strong mixed-income absorption in Brooklyn's coastal neighborhoods; this is a signal that inclusive housing + amenities-rich residential continues to absorb across NYC. For developers, this shows fitness/wellness anchors remain valuable lease-up tools in residential, particularly in underserved outer-borough markets.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Jonathan Stein of Douglas Elliman
stories.excerpt: For Jonathan Stein, the best is yet to come. Stein, 43, joined the real estate game in 2015 after spending time in the private equity space and then going on the road with his best friend’s rock band, Phantogram, as the tour manager. Now, he runs the Jonathan Stein Team at Douglas Elliman. Stein oversees a group of eight brokers at the firm, which has worked on deals ranging from $1 million to over $45 million. When former New York Mets and current Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Zack Wheeler needed to sell his SoHo penthouse at 73 Wooster Street, Stein and team member Gavin Shiminski stepped in, helping the major leaguer sell the unit for $26 million. It was one of the five largest sales in New York City in July. The road to such a successful real estate career wasn’t easy, but Stein said real estate is an amalgamation of his favorite things: design, architecture, mixing different personalities, and working well with people. “I got into real estate the old fashioned way — my life blew up and I needed a new career,” he said. “I was waiting tables at a buddy’s restaurant looking for what was going to come next. A friend suggested real estate and I loved the idea.” Commercial Observer caught up with Stein in August for “Get to Know the Broker,” a series where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What has been the biggest deal of your career? Jonathan Stein: I haven’t done it yet. Check back next year. What is your career Everest? Doing my own development project. What’s something you think people would be surprised to learn about you? I grew up on a farm in a town of 170 people. We raised cattle and pigs, and I showed pigs in 4-H as a kid to help earn money for college. What’s your go-to takeout order? Sushi from my neighborhood omakase spot. What TV show are you currently binging? “All Creatures Great and Small.” What is your silliest pet peeve? When
bullets: Broker profile of Jonathan Stein, Douglas Elliman, who closed $26M SoHo penthouse for MLB pitcher Zack Wheeler.
Stein leads eight-broker team; firm handles deals from $1M to $45M+ in Manhattan residential.
Article highlights broker career narrative and luxury sales activity; limited market signal.
stories.summary: Jonathan Stein, 43, leads the Jonathan Stein Team at Douglas Elliman, overseeing eight brokers focused on high-end Manhattan residential sales. Stein entered real estate in 2015 after private equity and tour management work. His team recently closed the $26 million sale of a SoHo penthouse for MLB pitcher Zack Wheeler, one of the five largest sales in New York City in July.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. High-end condop/luxury sales in SoHo reflect wealth concentration and capital mobility but do not signal multifamily demand or market conditions affecting apartments. Skip for strategic analysis.

stories.title: Rejection and Change Are Constants in Residential Brokerage. Adapt.
stories.excerpt: When I decided to get my real estate license, it’s safe to say I had no idea what I was in for. The perception of real estate agents is not the reality. A lot of people assume it’s about the money, but, for me, it’s really all about building and nurturing relationships. I’ve closed many deals by focusing on what was best for my clients, even when it required extra flexibility and problem-solving on my end. I realized early on that half the battle was just being available and accessible, and that building trust and transparency from the first call is key. As a young agent in the industry, I didn’t come into real estate with many connections. Most of my circle wasn’t ready to purchase a home or hire an agent for a rental. I had to find my own path, generating leads organically. But, as a young agent, I was extremely motivated to do so, and I was ready to adapt if needed. Mackenzie Kyle. PHOTO: Courtesy Platinum Properties One of my first deals was in the Financial District. My client’s mom found my profile on RentHop and called me out of the blue. We spoke about her search, and she asked if I could show an apartment in an hour. I lived an hour away from the building at this time, so I quickly rushed over. After a day of last-minute tours, I helped them find an apartment they loved. Their daughter was fresh out of school, and they were nervous about her moving to New York City, but, with my guidance and reassurance, they felt confident that the apartment was the right choice. I didn’t know this deal would jump-start my entire career, but it did. Not only do I still have an amazing relationship with these clients and have helped them find multiple homes, I was also connected with so many amazing referral clients from them because of the superior level of service that I provided. bullets: Essay on residential brokerage career advice: focus on relationships, adaptability, and organic lead generation.
Anecdote of young agent building Financial District business via RentHop profile and client referrals.
Thought-leadership piece on agent retention and professional development; no market signal.
stories.summary: An opinion piece by a residential agent sharing career lessons on the importance of building client relationships, maintaining transparency, and adapting to market change. The author recounts early career experiences generating leads organically through online platforms like RentHop and emphasizes availability and trust-building as core business drivers.
stories.impact: No relevance to multifamily development. This is industry commentary on brokerage business practices and agent retention, not market data. Skip for strategic analysis.
